cards.prompt: You type `example.org` into your browser. What must happen before any packet goes to the site?

options.text: DNS turns the name into an IP address
Routers read the name to choose a route
The site encrypts its name so nobody can read it
Your router gives example.org a private address

cards.explanation: Routers deliver by **IP address**, not by name, so your device first asks **DNS** for example.org's address, like a contacts app. Only then can packets go.

cards.prompt: Which of these names is controlled by whoever registered **example.org**?

options.text: news.example.org
example.org.news.example.com
example-org.example.net
news.example.org.example.net

cards.explanation: Read from the right: only `news.example.org` ends in **example.org**. The others end in `example.com` or `example.net`, whatever words they contain.

cards.prompt: No one has looked up example.com lately. Match each server to what it "says".
cards.explanation: The **resolver** asks for you, **root** points to the `.com` servers, **TLD** to example.com's own server, and only the **authoritative** server gives the real answer.

cards.prompt:
A site moves to a new address in 10 minutes, and its TTL is **3,600**.

Will devices that just looked it up switch right away?

options.text: No: they may use the old answer for up to an hour
Yes: every cache updates the moment the site moves
Yes: the TTL runs out before the 10 minutes do
No: they keep the old answer until restarted

cards.explanation: 3,600 seconds is **one hour**, longer than the 10 minutes, and nothing tells caches a site moved. But answers aren't kept forever, which is why owners lower the TTL before a move.

cards.prompt: Your browser looks up `shop.example.org`. The answer is a **CNAME** pointing to `example.org`. What happens next?

options.text: It looks up example.org to get an actual address
It connects to the name example.org straight away
It gives up, because the answer contained no address
It asks for shop.example.org's MX record instead

cards.explanation: A **CNAME** holds a name, and you can't connect to a name, so the lookup carries on with `example.org` to its **A** record. MX records are for email.

cards.prompt: Run `nslookup example.org` and find its **IPv4** address.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of example.org
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.org
Address: 203.0.113.80
Name:	example.org
Address: 2001:db8::80

cards.explanation: It's `203.0.113.80`. `2001:db8::80` is its IPv6 address, and `127.0.0.53` at the top is the DNS helper that answered.

cards.prompt: Visits to `example.org` and email to `hello@example.org` go to different machines. How does DNS do that?

options.text: An A record for the site, an MX record for email
A CNAME record sends email to the website server
Email skips DNS and finds its server another way
DNS holds one answer, so email needs a second domain

cards.explanation: One name can hold several **records**: **A** gives the site's address and **MX** names the mail server. A CNAME is just an alias.
